case_study_insert.main_stem: Westwind Rotor Refurbishment (WFR) is a private limited company in the wind energy and turbine-blade refurbishment sector, employing a workforce of 70. Founded in 2010 by Eleanor Brooks, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. WFR plans to invest $1,150,000 in a turbine-blade refurbishment plant with composite repair robotics, financed by a $750,000 ten-year bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $476,000 a year, a variable cost of $22 a unit and a selling price of $50, and currently produces 64,000 units a year. WFR also faces absenteeism of 10% and a rising blade-defect rate requiring rework, and aims to win more offshore service contracts next year.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and HR Report — Q3 2025: WFR serviced 4,200 blade units last quarter at a rework rate of 3.7%, up from 2.4% a year ago. Complaints about slow repairs rose from 23 to 38 per month, and average turnaround is 6.2 days. A survey of 340 wind-farm operators found that 74% value rapid blade repair and 63% would pay $4 more for a guaranteed fast turnaround. A skills audit shows 21 of 70 technicians need composite-repair training; an external course costs $1,250 per technician.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.2% to 5.0%, raising borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $15.00 to $15.89 per hour from January 2027. (3) Composite resin and carbon-fibre input costs have risen 12.1% year-on-year, while wind-farm service contracts grew 8.4% in the same period.

questions.question_text: WFR is funding part of its refurbishment-plant expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for WFR of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest payments or fixed repayments, so WFR keeps the cash that would otherwise service the $750,000 ten-year bank loan. That cash can cover fixed costs of $476,000 a year and the running of the new $1,150,000 refurbishment plant while absenteeism of 10% and a 3.7% rework rate are adding cost. Every dollar saved in interest can be spent on composite training or on reducing the 38 monthly complaints, helping WFR win offshore contracts without raising the $50 selling price.

Point 2: Using $400,000 retained profit keeps ownership and control with Eleanor Brooks's management rather than a lender, so no bank can impose conditions on how the composite repair robots are used. It also avoids pledging company assets while the 21 technicians still need $1,250 training and blades need rework. The survey evidence that 74% of operators value rapid repair and 63% would pay $4 more shows where internally saved cash can be reinvested, rather than paid as interest that competes with the $476,000 fixed costs and the cost of fixing the rising defect rate.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to WFR and its financing decision.

questions.question_text: WFR is promoting its new composite repair plant. Consider a wind-energy trade exhibition, search-engine advertising, or targeted social media and case-study webinars. Which should WFR choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Wind-energy trade exhibition: A stand at a wind-energy exhibition lets WFR demonstrate blade repair to operators and developers and build credibility in a technical market. However, stand, travel and staffing costs are high for a 70-employee firm already servicing a $750,000 loan and investing $1,150,000, and only a limited delegate audience attends, too narrow to support 64,000 units of output. It also does not directly tackle the 3.7% rework rate.

Search-engine advertising: Ads shown to people searching for blade repair reach high-intent buyers and can be tightly budget-controlled, which suits the 74% of surveyed operators who value rapid repair. The weakness is that text ads cannot demonstrate the composite robots or the guaranteed turnaround that 63% would pay $4 more for, and cost per click can rise quickly when a $1,150,000 investment must be justified.

Targeted social media and case-study webinars: Technical posts and live webinars can show before-and-after blade repairs and explain how the robots reduce the 3.7% rework rate, reaching wind-farm operators directly. This is low cost per contact and measurable, and it answers the 38 monthly complaints about slow repairs; webinars can also set out the 6.2-day turnaround and the 21 technicians needing $1,250 training, showing how capacity will grow.

Recommendation: WFR should choose targeted social media and case-study webinars. They demonstrate quality, reach the exact buyer and cost far less than a trade stand. The exhibition is rejected as expensive and narrow for a firm servicing a $750,000 loan; search advertising is rejected because it cannot demonstrate a technical service or reduce complaints. Webinars lack exhibition face-to-face contact, so WFR should add one regional exhibition stand once the rework rate is falling and the 10% absenteeism is under control.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to WFR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of WFR with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the exhibition and search ads are rejected.

questions.question_text: WFR has absenteeism of 10% and a rising blade-defect rate. Explain two benefits for WFR of using autocratic leadership within its hierarchical structure to improve reliability.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Eleanor Brooks set clear, uniform repair and inspection procedures for all 70 technicians, so everyone follows the same standard despite 10% absenteeism. In a hierarchical structure instructions pass down a defined chain of command, which reduces confusion when technicians are reassigned between blade jobs and helps hold the rework rate steady as the 3.7% defect problem grows.

Point 2: Quick, central decisions speed up responses to problems on the new $1,150,000 composite repair plant: managers can immediately reschedule a job or order materials when a repair fails, protecting the 4,200 quarterly blade units and the 6.2-day turnaround. Clear expectations also make it easy to identify which of the 21 technicians need the $1,250 course, so training is controlled. This decisiveness suits a business servicing a $750,000 loan, where delay is costly, and the 74% of operators valuing rapid repair can be assured standards are enforced. Autocratic leadership fits rule-based, time-critical work, allowing WFR to stabilise reliability before considering more participative methods.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WFR's absenteeism, defect rate and plant investment.

questions.question_text: WFR wants to cut its 10% absenteeism and 3.7% rework rate. Consider a performance-related bonus or job enrichment through team working. Which should WFR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Performance-related bonus: Paying technicians for defect-free repairs and full attendance could motivate the 70 staff to push the rework rate back from 3.7% toward 2.4% and shorten the 6.2-day turnaround, and it is easy to measure against the 4,200 quarterly blade units. However, the insert gives no bonus cost, so its expense cannot be calculated; it would add to fixed costs of $476,000 a year while WFR services a $750,000 loan and funds a $1,150,000 plant. A bonus also pays after defects occur and does not fix the repetitive work driving 10% absenteeism.

Job enrichment through team working: Giving technicians varied blade types, shared responsibility for composite repairs and a say in inspection routines makes work more interesting and uses their skills, which can cut the 3.7% rework rate at source. Team inspection can catch faults behind the 38 monthly complaints, and shared ownership can reduce 10% absenteeism by addressing its cause. Pairing the 21 technicians needing $1,250 training with experienced colleagues spreads skills. The drawback is the time needed to organise teams in a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership, and results may be slower than a bonus.

Decision: WFR should choose job enrichment through team working. It attacks the 10% absenteeism and 3.7% rework rate at source rather than paying around them, costs little compared with a bonus whose size is unstated, and helps the 21 technicians learn through colleagues. The bonus is rejected as an expensive short-term payment that does not change working methods, though a small bonus could be added once quality stabilises. With no stated bonus rate the comparison is qualitative: team working changes how the 70 technicians work, while a bonus only rewards results after the event and competes with $476,000 of fixed costs and the $750,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of a bonus and job enrichment with limited application to WFR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of WFR.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a well-justified decision covering absenteeism, cost, quality and motivation.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WFR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $476,000 ÷ ($50 − $22) = $476,000 ÷ $28 = 17,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 17,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $50 − $22 = $28. Answer: contribution per unit is $28.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WFR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 17,000-unit break-even output with 64,000 units refurbished, giving a margin of safety of 47,000 units, so managers can see how far offshore contracts could fall before the $1,150,000 plant stops covering costs.
2. Use the $28 contribution per unit to test the $4 premium that 63% of operators would pay: raising price to $54 gives $32 contribution and lowers break-even to 14,875 units (476,000 ÷ 32).
3. Average total cost is about $29.44 a unit ($476,000 ÷ 64,000 = $7.44 plus $22), below the $50 price, leaving room to absorb the 12.1% rise in resin and carbon-fibre costs without an immediate price rise.
4. Labour productivity is about 914 units per worker (64,000 ÷ 70), a benchmark for checking whether the $1,250 composite training and team working lift output despite 10% absenteeism.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 17,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $28 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 47,000 units; a $4 premium lifting contribution to $32 and lowering break-even to 14,875 units; average total cost of about $29.44 against the $50 price; labour productivity of about 914 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WFR's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin and the profit margin for 2024 and 2025. Has WFR's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 20.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 22.5%
ROCE 2024 = 15.7%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 revenue 1,100, cost of sales 660, gross profit 440; operating profit 220; capital employed 1,400. 2025 revenue 1,320, cost of sales 726, gross profit 594; operating profit 297; capital employed 1,650. Gross profit ÷ revenue: 440 ÷ 1,100 and 594 ÷ 1,320. Operating profit ÷ revenue: 220 ÷ 1,100 and 297 ÷ 1,320. Operating profit ÷ capital employed: 220 ÷ 1,400 and 297 ÷ 1,650.

Evaluation: Every measure is higher in 2025. The share of revenue left after direct costs rose from 40.0% to 45.0% because revenue grew by 220 while cost of sales rose by only 66, so the refurbishment service is becoming more efficient despite the 3.7% rework rate. The share retained as operating profit also rose, and the return on the 1,650 of capital employed improved, which matters because WFR must service a $750,000 loan while investing $1,150,000 in the new plant. Interest payable of 42 in 2025 is modest beside operating profit of 297, so financing costs are not undermining the gain. The 10% absenteeism and 38 monthly complaints remain risks that could reverse the trend if quality slips.

Conclusion: WFR's financial position has improved. Both margins and the return on capital are higher, with revenue growing much faster than cost of sales. Management should use the stronger margins to fund composite training and quality checks so that absenteeism and defects do not erase the improvement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the two margins for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, profit and capital trends, and a justified conclusion on whether WFR improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WFR of introducing composite repair robotics at its refurbishment plant.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Composite robots can make repairs more consistent, helping push the rework rate from 3.7% back toward 2.4% and cutting the 38 monthly complaints about slow repairs. Combined with the survey finding that 74% of wind-farm operators value rapid blade repair and 63% would pay $4 more for a guaranteed turnaround, better quality can protect the $50 selling price, the $28 contribution per unit and the 64,000-unit output.

Disadvantage: The $1,150,000 plant must be financed alongside a $750,000 loan, and the 21 technicians needing $1,250 training cannot operate the robots until trained, which is difficult with 10% absenteeism. The insert gives no figure for robot maintenance or energy use, so the exact cost saving cannot be calculated; only a qualitative comparison with the $22 variable cost is possible. If the robots fail, the 4,200 quarterly blade units and the 6.2-day turnaround could be disrupted, so quality gains depend on reliable operation and training before offshore contracts are won.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WFR's survey, defect rate and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase to $15.89 and the 12.1% rise in composite resin and carbon-fibre costs will affect WFR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.2% to 5.0%): If WFR's $750,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.8% × $750,000 = $6,000 a year, shown as 0.008 × $750,000. This is modest against $476,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the direct cost is zero. Higher rates may still slow the 8.4% growth in wind-farm service contracts.

Minimum wage increase (5.9% to $15.89 an hour): The insert gives no hours worked or current pay, so an annual wage cost cannot be invented. The derived measure is productivity: 64,000 units ÷ 70 workers = about 914 units per worker. If that holds, the wage rise can be absorbed; if the 10% absenteeism and 3.7% rework rate reduce effective output, unit labour costs rise and the $28 contribution falls. The direction is clear but the size cannot be quantified here.

Input-cost inflation (12.1%): The $22 variable cost is not split into components, so an explicit upper bound is 12.1% × $22 = $2.662, about $2.66 per unit. Across 64,000 units that is 64,000 × $2.66 = $170,240 a year. Even a smaller rise cuts contribution from $28 toward about $25.34 and pushes the break-even output above 17,000 units.

Conclusion: The 12.1% rise in composite resin and carbon-fibre costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 64,000 units and directly erodes the $28 contribution that must cover $476,000 fixed costs and service the $750,000 loan, whereas the interest rise is about $6,000 and the wage effect is unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity. WFR can recover part of it through the $4 premium that 63% of operators accept, but that premium is unlikely to cover a cost rise of roughly $170,240 a year.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to WFR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on WFR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.
